SKILLS.note: Weight in the heels, hips below the knees, lumbar curve held.
Midline as rigid as a plank. Chest to deck, arms to full lockout.
Static core, hips and shoulders rise together, bar tracks the legs.
Strict press, no leg drive. Finish with the head through the window.
Hands touch the floor overhead, then touch the feet.
Where every pull begins. Body in one line, rings to the chest.
Wide stance. Power moves hips to arms, and the arms bend last.
The teaching model for the clean. Explode, then drop under to receive.
Chest and thighs to the floor, jump, clap overhead.
Chin over the bar with no kip. The gate to every advanced pull.
Earn the strict version first, then add the arch-hollow rhythm.
Continuous cycling. Fastest rep rate, least margin for error.
Same pull, higher finish. The chest makes real contact.
Kip plus range. Pull to the sternum, not the collarbone.
Shoulders below the elbows at the bottom, full lockout on top.
Unstable support. A required part before any ring muscle-up.
Below the bar to above it in one motion. Hips to bar, then push away.
Pure strength. No kip to carry you through the transition.
On rings. Timing of the turnover is everything.
One of the true end points of the gymnastics tree.
From a hang to front support over the bar.
Seated or standing start. Learn the foot lock before the height.
Wrapping or basket lock. The legs should do half the work.
Upper body only. Grip is usually the limiter, not the pull.
Legless, with the legs held at ninety degrees.
Rings turn out at the top, shoulders stay packed.
Feet up the wall, hands walk in. Builds the inverted position.
Push tall through the shoulders, ribs down. Hold thirty seconds first.
Head to the floor, press to full lockout, no kip.
Tuck then drive. The hips help the shoulders finish.
Extra range from plates or blocks. A shoulder endurance test.
Shift the weight slightly past the hands and take small steps.
Turn on one hand while inverted. Spatial control under fatigue.
No wall. Balance and strength at the same time.
Hang without swinging. Knees make contact with the elbows.
Legs straight, toes touch the bar between the hands.
Arch and hollow. Rhythm beats effort here.
Controlled inversion on rings. Builds shoulder end-range strength.
Legs parallel to the floor. A hard, honest midline benchmark.
Same shape, unstable support.
Hold the L while pulling. Nothing to hide behind.
Progress slowly. Do not go big on the first exposure.
Rotate the legs side to side while hanging.
Full depth on one leg. The other never touches down.
Bar on the traps, hips below the knees, drive the whole foot.
Elbows high, bar supported by the front rack, not the hands.
The foundation of the snatch. Tests shoulders, t-spine and ankles at once.
Bar in the crook of the elbows. Brutal on the midline.
Shoulder blades retracted, bar touches the chest, feet planted.
One shallow dip and drive. The legs start it, the arms finish it.
Second dip to receive. Arms are already locked when you catch it.
Split the feet to receive. The heaviest overhead position available.
Front squat into push press, one continuous movement. The classic.
Press from the bottom of a squat. Mobility work disguised as a lift.
From above the knee. Receive with the hips above parallel.
From the floor, caught high. Speed under the bar beats pull height.
Hang start, full squat receive.
Floor to front rack in a full squat. More weight than the power version.
Receive in a split stance. Rare in class, useful for footwork.
One of the two Olympic lifts.
No dip under. Pull and turn the bar over to lockout.
Hang start, caught above parallel.
Floor to overhead, caught high.
Hang start, full squat receive.
Floor to overhead in one motion, full squat. The hardest lift in the sport.
Trains speed under the bar and overhead stability.
Wide stance, hands inside the knees.
Hip hinge with the bar on the back. Start far lighter than you think.
A hip hinge, not a squat and not an arm raise.
One motion to overhead. Punch through so it does not bang the wrist.
Back knee lightly touches, torso upright.
Load in the front rack. The midline has to hold the position.
Bar on the back. Heavier than the front rack version.
The most demanding lunge for overhead stability.
Slow, controlled, eyes on the weight the whole way.
Shoulders down and back. Do not shrug the load.
Turn the rope with the wrists, not the arms.
Jump a little higher, spin a little faster, stay relaxed.
Legs, hips, arms on the drive. Reverse it on the recovery.
Midfoot strike, lean from the ankles, high cadence.
Body position first. Efficiency beats effort in the water.
Whole foot on the box, stand to full extension.
Land soft, open the hips at the top.
Pace over speed. This one punishes an early sprint.
Full squat, hit the target, catch and go straight back down.
Full extension overhead, then drive it into the floor.
Roll back, kick over, stand and jump.
